title: Plant Kingdom – Day 3 Lesson
introduction: This lesson covers the major plant groups from algae to angiosperms, their distinguishing features, evolutionary significance, and the various plant life‑cycle patterns examined in NEET‑UG.

sections.heading: Algae – General Characteristics and Major Classes
sections.content: Algae are primarily aquatic, photosynthetic organisms ranging from unicellular micro‑algae to large multicellular seaweeds. They possess chlorophyll a and accessory pigments, store starch, and have cell walls of cellulose or agar. Major classes: Chlorophyceae (green algae) – e.g., Chlamydomonas, Ulva; Phaeophyceae (brown algae) – e.g., Laminaria, Fucus; Rhodophyceae (red algae) – e.g., Porphyra, Gracilaria. Economically important for food (spirulina, nori), fertilizers, agar, carrageenan, and biofuels.
keyPoints: Aquatic, photosynthetic, chlorophyll a present in all.
Chlorophyceae: chlorophyll b, store starch, cell walls of cellulose.
Phaeophyceae: fucoxanthin gives brown colour, store laminarin, cell walls of alginates.
Rhodophyceae: phycoerythrin gives red colour, lack flagella, store floridean starch.
Uses: food, industrial polysaccharides, fertilizers, biofuel precursors.
neetTips: Remember pigment combinations to identify classes.
Link economic products (agar‑Rhodophyceae, alginate‑Phaeophyceae).
NEET often asks about storage products and cell‑wall constituents.

sections.heading: Bryophytes – Non‑vascular Land Plants
sections.content: Bryophytes are the simplest terrestrial plants lacking true vascular tissue. They consist of a dominant gametophyte and a dependent sporophyte. Two major groups: Liverworts (Marchantiophyta) – thalloid or leafy, rhizoids for anchorage; Mosses (Bryophyta) – leafy shoots with a simple stem‑leaf arrangement. They require moist habitats, a trait shared with many amphibians, facilitating water‑dependent fertilisation.
keyPoints: Dominant gametophyte; sporophyte attached to gametophyte.
No true xylem or phloem; water and nutrients conducted by diffusion.
Liverworts: oil bodies, simple thallus; Mosses: leaf‑like phyllids, rhizoids.
Reproduction via water‑mediated sperm motility.
neetTips: Identify the dominant phase (gametophyte) for bryophytes.
Recall that absence of vascular tissue distinguishes them from pteridophytes.
Link moist habitat requirement to amphibian ecology for conceptual questions.

sections.heading: Pteridophytes – Vascular Seedless Plants
sections.content: Pteridophytes possess true xylem and phloem, allowing larger size and colonisation of drier habitats. They exhibit a dominant sporophyte and a free‑living, usually reduced, gametophyte (prothallus). Major groups include ferns and horsetails. Heterospory – production of distinct microspores (male) and megaspores (female) – first appears in some pteridophytes (e.g., Selaginella).
keyPoints: True vascular tissue (tracheids, sieve elements).
Life cycle: dominant sporophyte, independent gametophyte.
Heterospory: microspores → male gametophyte; megaspores → female gametophyte.
Examples: Ferns (Polypodiopsida), Horsetails (Equisetopsida).
neetTips: Remember heterospory as a key evolutionary step toward seed plants.
Distinguish between homosporous (most ferns) and heterosporous pteridophytes.
NEET may ask about vascular tissue types in pteridophytes.

sections.heading: Gymnosperms – Naked Seed Plants
sections.content: Gymnosperms are seed‑bearing plants with ovules exposed on cone scales (naked seeds). They are heterosporous, producing microspores in pollen cones and megaspores in ovulate cones. Major groups: Conifers (Pinus, Abies), Cycads, Ginkgo, Gnetales. Seeds contain a nutritive tissue (albumen) and a protective integument, but lack a fruit.
keyPoints: Naked seeds on cone scales; no enclosing ovary.
Heterospory with distinct male (pollen) and female (ovule) cones.
Vascular tissue: tracheids for water transport; sieve‑tube elements for photosynthate.
Adaptations: resin canals, thick cuticle, sunken stomata.
neetTips: Link ‘gymnosperm’ to ‘naked seed’ – no fruit.
Recall that conifers dominate boreal forests – useful for ecological questions.
Focus on heterospory and cone morphology for NEET.

sections.heading: Angiosperms – Flowering Plants
sections.content: Angiosperms are the most advanced plant group, characterised by seeds enclosed within a fruit (ovary). They are heterosporous with flowers containing stamens (microsporangia) and carpels (megasporangia). Two major classes: Monocotyledons (single cotyledon, parallel leaf venation, scattered vascular bundles) and Dicotyledons (two cotyledons, netted venation, ring‑arranged vascular bundles).
keyPoints: Enclosed seeds – ovary develops into fruit.
Flower structure: sepals, petals, stamens, carpels.
Monocots: 1 cotyledon, parallel veins, fibrous roots.
Dicots: 2 cotyledons, reticulate veins, taproot system.
neetTips: Memorise monocot vs dicot leaf‑venation and vascular bundle arrangement.
Fruit type (simple, aggregate) often asked – focus on ovary position.
Remember that double fertilisation produces endosperm (triploid).

sections.heading: Plant Life Cycles – Dominant Phases
sections.content: Plant life cycles are described by the relative dominance of haploid (gametophyte) and diploid (sporophyte) phases. Three patterns occur: haplontic (haploid dominant), diplontic (diploid dominant), and haplo‑diplontic (both phases free‑living, as in most land plants). The alternation of generations links these phases through meiosis and fertilisation.
keyPoints: Haplontic: only gametophyte is multicellular (e.g., many algae).
Diplontic: only sporophyte is multicellular (e.g., animals, some algae).
Haplo‑diplontic: both phases multicellular – typical of land plants.
Meiosis produces spores; fertilisation restores diploidy.
neetTips: NEET often asks to identify the life‑cycle type from a diagram.
Remember that the dominant phase shifts from algae → bryophytes → vascular plants.

sections.heading: Alternation of Generations – Gametophyte ↔ Sporophyte
sections.content: Alternation of generations is the cyclic transition between a haploid gametophyte and a diploid sporophyte. The sporophyte undergoes meiosis to produce haploid spores, which develop into gametophytes. Gametophytes produce gametes by mitosis; fusion of gametes (fertilisation) restores the diploid sporophyte. In bryophytes the gametophyte is dominant; in pteridophytes, gymnosperms and angiosperms the sporophyte dominates.
keyPoints: Meiosis → spores (haploid).
Spore germination → gametophyte (mitosis).
Gametes → fertilisation → zygote → sporophyte.
Shift in dominance across plant evolution.
neetTips: Identify which phase is dominant for each plant group.
Diagrammatic representation is a common NEET question.

sections.heading: Haplontic Life Cycle – Predominantly Haploid
sections.content: In a haplontic cycle, the multicellular organism is haploid; diploid stage exists only as a short‑lived zygote that undergoes immediate meiosis to produce haploid spores. This pattern is typical of many unicellular algae (e.g., Chlamydomonas).
keyPoints: Multicellular stage = haploid.
Zygote undergoes meiosis without growth.
Common in many green algae.
neetTips: Remember that the sporophyte is absent or reduced to a zygote.
NEET may contrast haplontic algae with diplontic algae.

sections.heading: Diplontic Life Cycle – Predominantly Diploid
sections.content: In a diplontic cycle, the multicellular organism is diploid; haploid cells are limited to gametes. The only haploid stage is the gamete, which fuses to form a diploid zygote that develops directly into the sporophyte. This pattern is seen in most animals and some brown algae (e.g., Fucus).
keyPoints: Multicellular stage = diploid.
Haploid stage restricted to gametes.
Zygote grows directly into sporophyte.
neetTips: Distinguish from haplontic by noting presence of a true multicellular sporophyte.
Brown algae (Fucus) exemplify diplontic life cycle.

sections.heading: Haplo‑Diplontic Life Cycle – Both Phases Free‑Living
sections.content: The haplo‑diplontic cycle features independent, multicellular haploid (gametophyte) and diploid (sporophyte) generations. This is the hallmark of land plants. The sporophyte produces spores by meiosis; spores develop into gametophytes, which produce gametes by mitosis. Fertilisation restores the diploid sporophyte.
keyPoints: Both gametophyte and sporophyte are multicellular.
Sporophyte dominant in vascular plants; gametophyte dominant in bryophytes.
Meiosis → spores; mitosis → gametophyte; fertilisation → sporophyte.
neetTips: NEET often asks which plant groups exhibit haplo‑diplontic cycles.
Remember the shift in dominance from bryophytes to angiosperms.

learningOutcome: Identify and compare the major plant groups and understand their evolutionary progression and life-cycle patterns.

mcqs.question: Which pigment gives brown algae (Phaeophyceae) their characteristic colour, distinguishing them from green algae?
mcqs.explanation: Brown algae contain the brown‑coloured pigment fucoxanthin, masking chlorophylls, whereas green algae lack this pigment.

mcqs.question: In the life cycle of a typical moss, which generation is nutritionally independent and dominant?
mcqs.explanation: Mosses exhibit a gametophyte‑dominant (haploid) life cycle; the sporophyte remains attached to and depends on the gametophyte.

mcqs.question: Heterospory, the production of two distinct spores, first evolved in which plant group?
mcqs.explanation: True heterospory appears in some pteridophytes such as Selaginella, predating its widespread occurrence in gymnosperms.

mcqs.question: Which statement about monocotyledonous angiosperms is FALSE?
options: Vascular bundles are scattered in the stem
Flowers usually have parts in multiples of three
mcqs.explanation: Monocots generally lack a vascular cambium, so secondary growth is rare; the other statements are true for monocots.

mcqs.question: Which feature most clearly distinguishes bryophytes from pteridophytes?
mcqs.explanation: Bryophytes lack true vascular tissue and have rhizoids for anchorage, whereas pteridophytes possess well‑developed vascular bundles (xylem and phloem).

mcqs.question: In a typical moss, the part of the sporophyte that penetrates the gametophyte to obtain nutrients is called the:
mcqs.explanation: The foot is the basal region of the sporophyte that grows into the gametophytic tissue, allowing transfer of water and nutrients.

mcqs.question: The group of algae that shares the closest chloroplast structure and pigment composition with bryophytes is:
mcqs.explanation: Chlorophyceae (green algae) have chloroplasts containing chlorophyll a, b and carotenoids, similar to the chloroplasts of bryophytes, indicating a close evolutionary relationship.

mcqs.question: Which statement about the dominant generation in bryophytes is correct?
options: The sporophyte generation is diploid and photosynthetic
The gametophyte generation is haploid and photosynthetic
The sporophyte generation is haploid and non‑photosynthetic
The gametophyte generation is diploid and non‑photosynthetic
mcqs.explanation: In bryophytes the gametophyte is the conspicuous, photosynthetic, haploid phase, while the sporophyte is smaller, diploid and nutritionally dependent on the gametophyte.

mcqs.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes gymnosperms from angiosperms?
options: Gymnosperms bear seeds enclosed within an ovary
Gymnosperms possess vessel elements in their xylem
Gymnosperms produce pollen in microsporangia of male cones
mcqs.explanation: Gymnosperms produce pollen grains in the microsporangia of male cones, whereas angiosperms produce pollen in anthers of flowers. The other statements describe angiosperm traits.

mcqs.question: Which extant gymnosperm is the sole representative of its division and bears ovules on the surface of a fleshy, seed‑like megasporophyll?
mcqs.explanation: Ginkgo biloba, the only living member of Ginkgoales, has ovules borne on a fleshy megasporophyll. Gnetum, Cycas, and Pinus belong to other gymnosperm groups.

mcqs.question: Gymnosperm wood is primarily composed of which type of water‑conducting cell, distinguishing it from most angiosperm wood?
mcqs.explanation: Gymnosperm xylem consists mainly of tracheids for water transport and support. Angiosperm wood typically contains vessel elements, which are absent in most gymnosperms.

mcqs.question: Which structural adaptation most directly enables many gymnosperms to survive in cold, dry environments?
options: Presence of resin canals in stems and leaves
mcqs.explanation: Resin canals produce terpenoid resins that protect against desiccation, herbivory, and freezing injury, aiding gymnosperms in harsh, xeric or cold habitats. The other options are not characteristic of gymnosperms.

mcqs.question: Which plant group exhibits a dominant sporophyte phase and heterospory?
mcqs.explanation: Gymnosperms have a conspicuous diploid sporophyte and produce two distinct types of spores (microspores and megaspores), i.e., heterospory.

mcqs.question: In the typical haplo‑diplontic life cycle of a fern, what are the ploidy levels of the gametophyte and sporophyte respectively?
mcqs.explanation: The fern gametophyte (prothallus) is haploid (n) and gives rise to gametes, while the sporophyte that develops after fertilisation is diploid (2n).

mcqs.question: Which statement correctly describes the life cycle of a typical moss (Bryophyte)?
mcqs.explanation: Mosses have a conspicuous haploid gametophyte that carries out most of the life functions; the diploid sporophyte is short‑lived and dependent, reflecting a haplontic cycle.

mcqs.question: In a typical diploid‑dominant plant such as an angiosperm, which generation is nutritionally independent and carries out photosynthesis?
mcqs.explanation: Angiosperms have a dominant sporophyte that is free‑living, photosynthetic and nutritionally independent, whereas the gametophyte is reduced and dependent.

mcqs.question: Heterosporous plants (e.g., most gymnosperms and pteridophytes) differ from homosporous plants because they:
options: Produce isomorphic spores of the same size
mcqs.explanation: Heterospory is the production of two distinct spore types: microspores (male) and megaspores (female), each developing into separate gametophytes.

mcqs.question: In the life cycle of a fern, the specialized structure that bears the sporangia on the undersurface of the frond is called:
mcqs.explanation: A sorus (plural sori) is a cluster of sporangia on the underside of fern fronds where meiosis occurs to produce spores.

mcqs.question: In a haplontic life cycle, which cell is the only diploid stage?
mcqs.explanation: In haplontic organisms (many algae), the diploid stage is limited to the zygote, which undergoes meiosis directly to give haploid cells.

mcqs.question: Which of the following organisms is a classic example of a haplontic life cycle?
mcqs.explanation: Chlamydomonas (a unicellular green alga) has a haplontic cycle where the dominant phase is haploid and the only diploid stage is the zygote.

mcqs.question: In a haplontic life cycle, the phase that persists for the longest period is:
mcqs.explanation: The haploid gametophyte (or vegetative haploid organism) is the long‑lived stage; the diploid zygote undergoes meiosis immediately.

mcqs.question: During the haplontic life cycle, meiosis takes place:
options: Immediately after fertilization, converting the diploid zygote into haploid cells
Meiosis does not occur in haplontic organisms
mcqs.explanation: In haplontic organisms, the diploid zygote undergoes meiosis right after fertilization to produce haploid cells, so the diploid stage is transient.

mcqs.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes a haplontic cycle from a diplontic cycle?
options: In haplontic life cycles the zygote undergoes mitosis to form a multicellular diploid organism
In diplontic cycles haploid spores give rise to a gametophyte
In haplontic cycles the only diploid stage is the zygote
In diplontic cycles meiosis occurs only in the gametophyte
mcqs.explanation: In haplontic cycles the zygote is the sole diploid phase and immediately undergoes meiosis; diplontic cycles have a persistent diploid multicellular organism.

mcqs.question: In a diplontic life cycle, which phase constitutes the conspicuous, multicellular organism that we commonly recognize?
options: Both haploid and diploid phases equally
mcqs.explanation: Diplontic life cycles are characterized by a dominant diploid sporophyte; the haploid gametophyte is reduced to unicellular gametes.

mcqs.question: What type of cell division gives rise to haploid gametes in a diplontic plant?
mcqs.explanation: Meiosis reduces the chromosome number from diploid (2n) to haploid (n), producing the male and female gametes.

mcqs.question: Which of the following plant groups primarily exhibits a diplontic life cycle?
mcqs.explanation: Gymnosperms (and angiosperms) have a diplontic life cycle where the diploid sporophyte is the main plant body; bryophytes and pteridophytes are haplontic or haplo‑diplontic.

mcqs.question: Immediately after fertilization in a diplontic organism, the zygote is:
mcqs.explanation: Fertilization fuses two haploid gametes, restoring the diploid chromosome number (2n) in the zygote, which then develops into the sporophyte.

mcqs.question: In a haplo‑diplontic life cycle, which statement correctly describes the relative prominence of the sporophyte and gametophyte in most land plants?
options: Sporophyte is multicellular and dominant, while gametophyte is reduced and often dependent.
Gametophyte is multicellular and dominant, while sporophyte is reduced.
Both sporophyte and gametophyte are equally conspicuous.
Neither phase is multicellular; both are unicellular.
mcqs.explanation: Most land plants (bryophytes to angiosperms) have a haplo‑diplontic cycle where the diploid sporophyte is the conspicuous, photosynthetic generation and the haploid gametophyte is reduced and nutritionally dependent.

mcqs.question: In the haplo‑diplontic life cycle of a typical fern (a pteridophyte), spores are produced by which process and in which structure?
options: Meiosis in the sporangia of the sporophyte.
Mitosis in the archegonia of the gametophyte.
Meiosis in the antheridia of the gametophyte.
Mitosis in the rhizome of the sporophyte.
mcqs.explanation: Ferns produce haploid spores by meiosis within sporangia that are borne on the fronds of the diploid sporophyte. These spores germinate into the free‑living gametophyte.

mcqs.question: Which photosynthetic pigment is characteristically absent in members of the class Chlorophyceae?
mcqs.explanation: Green algae (Chlorophyceae) contain chlorophyll a, chlorophyll b, carotenoids and xanthophylls, but lack the phycobilin pigments (phycoerythrin, phycocyanin) that are typical of red and brown algae.

mcqs.question: The principal storage product accumulated in the vegetative cells of Chlorophyceae is:
mcqs.explanation: Chlorophyceae store photosynthate as starch granules, similar to higher plants. Laminarin is typical of brown algae, floridean starch of red algae, and glycogen is a storage polysaccharide of many fungi and animals.

mcqs.question: Which of the following best describes the composition of the cell wall in Chlorophyceae?
mcqs.explanation: The cell walls of green algae are primarily composed of cellulose fibers embedded in a matrix of pectic substances, resembling the primary walls of land plants. Silica and calcium carbonate are characteristic of diatoms and some marine algae, while sulphated polysaccharides are typical of red algae.

mcqs.question: Which pigment is primarily responsible for the characteristic red colour of Rhodophyceae and is absent in Chlorophyceae?
mcqs.explanation: Rhodophyceae contain the accessory pigment phycoerythrin, which absorbs green light and imparts a red hue; this pigment is not found in Chlorophyceae.

mcqs.question: The principal storage polysaccharide in Rhodophyceae is:
mcqs.explanation: Red algae store carbohydrates as floridean starch, a β‑1,3‑glucan, unlike the amylose/amylopectin starch of green plants.

mcqs.question: Which commercially important product is extracted mainly from members of the Rhodophyceae?
mcqs.explanation: Agar, a gelatinous polysaccharide used in microbiology and food industry, is obtained from red algae such as Gelidium and Gracilaria.

mcqs.question: The typical life cycle of most Rhodophyceae is best described as:
mcqs.explanation: Red algae exhibit a triphasic (haplo‑diplontic) life cycle comprising a haploid gametophyte, a diploid carposporophyte, and a diploid tetrasporophyte.

mcqs.question: Which characteristic most clearly distinguishes bryophytes from pteridophytes?
mcqs.explanation: Bryophytes have a dominant haploid gametophyte stage, whereas pteridophytes have a dominant diploid sporophyte and possess vascular tissues.
mcqs.topic: Bryophytes and amphibians of plant kingdom

mcqs.question: In a typical moss life cycle, the sporangium that bears spores is formed by which generation?
options: Neither generation; it is a separate structure
mcqs.explanation: The sporangium (capsule) is part of the diploid sporophyte, which grows attached to the haploid gametophyte and releases spores.
mcqs.topic: Bryophytes and amphibians of plant kingdom

mcqs.question: Molecular and pigment evidence suggests that the closest algal relatives of land bryophytes belong to which class?
mcqs.explanation: Charophyceae (charophyte algae) share similar chlorophyll a+b ratios, cell wall components, and DNA sequences with embryophytes, indicating they are the nearest algal ancestors of bryophytes.
mcqs.topic: Bryophytes and amphibians of plant kingdom

mcqs.question: Which statement about water relations in bryophytes is correct?
options: They possess a cuticle thicker than most angiosperms
They rely on capillary action for internal water transport
They regulate transpiration through stomata that open only at night
mcqs.explanation: Bryophytes lack true vascular tissue; water moves by capillary action and diffusion through their thin tissues, making them dependent on a moist environment.
mcqs.topic: Bryophytes and amphibians of plant kingdom

mcqs.question: In the life cycle of mosses, which generation is dominant and primarily responsible for photosynthesis?
mcqs.explanation: Mosses have a haploid gametophyte that is long‑lived, green, and photosynthetic, whereas the sporophyte is short‑lived and dependent on the gametophyte.

mcqs.question: The part of a moss sporophyte that penetrates the gametophyte tissue and absorbs nutrients is called the:
mcqs.explanation: The foot is a basal structure of the sporophyte that grows into the gametophyte, anchoring it and facilitating transfer of water and nutrients.

mcqs.question: Which characteristic most clearly separates mosses (Bryophyta) from liverworts (Marchantiophyta)?
options: Presence of peristome teeth around the capsule opening
Presence of a dominant gametophyte generation
mcqs.explanation: Most mosses possess a peristome – a ring of teeth that regulate spore release – a feature generally absent in liverworts.

mcqs.question: Mosses are economically important for all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Acting as bio‑indicators of air quality
Providing microhabitats for forest floor fauna
mcqs.explanation: Commercial polysaccharides are extracted from algae, not from mosses; the other options are recognized uses of mosses.

mcqs.question: Heterospory is the production of two distinct types of spores, microspores and megaspores, which develop into male and female gametophytes respectively. Which of the following plant groups is NOT heterosporous?
mcqs.explanation: Bryophytes are homosporous; they produce a single type of spore that gives rise to a bisexual gametophyte. All the other listed groups exhibit heterospory.

mcqs.question: The evolution of heterospory is considered a key step towards the development of seeds because:
options: It allows separation of male and female gametophytes in time
It results in larger megaspores that can retain nutritive tissue
It eliminates the need for water for fertilization
It increases the number of spores produced per sporangium
mcqs.explanation: Larger megaspores in heterosporous plants can develop nutritive tissue (megagametophyte) that supports the embryo, a fundamental feature of seed plants.

mcqs.question: In heterosporous lycophytes such as Selaginella, the structures that bear microspores are:
mcqs.explanation: Microsporangia are produced on strobili (cone-like structures) in heterosporous lycophytes, separating them from megasporangia.

mcqs.question: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of monocotyledonous plants?
options: Scattered vascular bundles in the stem
mcqs.explanation: Monocots have parallel leaf venation; net‑like (reticulate) venation is typical of dicots.

mcqs.question: In a typical dicot leaf, the arrangement of vascular bundles is:
options: Collateral with xylem towards the adaxial side
Collateral with xylem towards the abaxial side
mcqs.explanation: In dicot leaves, vascular bundles are collateral; the xylem is positioned toward the upper (adaxial) surface and phloem toward the lower (abaxial) surface.

mcqs.question: Regarding the dominance of generations in flowering plants, which statement is correct?
options: Both monocots and dicots have a dominant sporophyte generation
Monocots have a dominant gametophyte generation
Dicots exhibit a haplontic life cycle
Monocots show alternation of generations with a dominant gametophyte
mcqs.explanation: All angiosperms, whether monocots or dicots, have a dominant diploid sporophyte; the gametophyte is reduced and short‑lived.

mcqs.question: Which floral formula best represents a typical monocot flower?
mcqs.explanation: Monocot flowers are usually trimerous, i.e., parts occur in multiples of three, giving the formula *[3+3] (e.g., three sepals, three petals).

mcqs.question: In which plant group is the sporophyte the dominant, diploid phase and the gametophyte highly reduced, while the plant exhibits heterospory?
mcqs.explanation: Gymnosperms have a dominant diploid sporophyte, a minute gametophyte, and produce two distinct spores (microspores and megaspores), i.e., they are heterosporous.

mcqs.question: In the life cycle of a typical moss, which statement correctly describes the ploidy of the dominant phase?
options: The dominant phase is diploid sporophyte
The dominant phase is haploid gametophyte
Both gametophyte and sporophyte are equally prominent
The dominant phase is diploid gametophyte
mcqs.explanation: Mosses (bryophytes) have a dominant haploid gametophyte; the sporophyte remains attached to and nutritionally dependent on the gametophyte.

mcqs.question: Which description best fits the alternation of generations in a homosporous fern?
options: It produces two types of spores, microspores and megaspores
The diploid sporophyte produces identical spores that develop into a free‑living, photosynthetic gametophyte
mcqs.explanation: In homosporous ferns, the diploid sporophyte undergoes meiosis to produce one type of spore; each spore grows into a small, independent, photosynthetic haploid gametophyte (prothallus).

mcqs.question: In a haplontic life cycle, which stage undergoes meiosis?
mcqs.explanation: In a haplontic life cycle, the only diploid cell is the zygote, which immediately undergoes meiosis to give rise to haploid cells, so meiosis occurs in the zygote.
